raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the prototypical angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI). Its development followed disappointment with vasopeptidase inhibition: omapatrilat improved some haemodynamic and clinical signals but excess angioedema limited its use, underscoring the need to avoid simultaneous angiotensin-converting enzyme and neprilysin inhibition [1]. Sacubitril/valsartan combines neprilysin inhibition, which augments natriuretic peptides, bradykinin and other vasoactive substrates, with valsartan-mediated angiotensin II type-1 receptor blockade. The PARADIGM-HF programme was designed to test whether this dual pathway would outperform established renin–angiotensin system inhibition in chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [2].

The pivotal PARADIGM-HF trial transformed HFrEF therapy. In ambulatory patients with symptomatic HFrEF and elevated natriuretic peptides, sacubitril/valsartan reduced cardiovascular death or first heart-failure hospitalisation versus enalapril, and also reduced all-cause mortality [3]. Subsequent analyses suggested that benefit was not confined to prevention of first events: sacubitril/valsartan reduced clinical progression among survivors [4], sudden death and pump-failure death [5], and maintained efficacy in older patients despite more hypotension [6]. Importantly, it appeared compatible with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, with less severe hyperkalaemia than enalapril in one secondary analysis [7]. In patients with diabetes, sacubitril/valsartan was associated with modestly improved glycaemic control and less initiation of insulin therapy, a hypothesis-generating finding that reinforced the systemic effects of neurohormonal modulation [8]. Reduced loop-diuretic requirement during follow-up further suggested improved congestion biology rather than simple event suppression [9].

Initiation during or soon after hospitalisation has been a major practical question. PIONEER-HF showed that, in haemodynamically stable patients hospitalised for acute decompensated HFrEF, in-hospital sacubitril/valsartan produced a larger fall in NT-proBNP than enalapril without excess worsening renal function, hyperkalaemia or symptomatic hypotension [10]. High-risk subgroups, including patients with de novo heart failure, lower systolic blood pressure or impaired renal function, showed broadly consistent efficacy and safety [11]. TITRATION demonstrated that both condensed and conservative uptitration strategies were feasible, although slower titration may be better tolerated in patients not previously receiving high-dose renin–angiotensin system inhibition [12]. TRANSITION extended this concept by showing that pre-discharge and early post-discharge initiation were both feasible after stabilisation [13]. In routine care, these data support starting ARNI before therapeutic inertia develops, provided blood pressure, renal function and potassium are monitored.

Reverse remodelling provides biological plausibility for improved outcomes. In PROVE-HF, reduction in NT-proBNP after sacubitril/valsartan initiation correlated with improvements in left ventricular volumes and ejection fraction [14]. EVALUATE-HF did not show a significant effect on central aortic stiffness, but did show favourable cardiac structural changes [15]. In selected patients with functional mitral regurgitation, sacubitril/valsartan reduced regurgitant volume more than valsartan, consistent with ventricular unloading and remodelling effects [16]. However, advanced HFrEF remains challenging: the LIFE trial in patients with very advanced disease did not show a clear advantage over valsartan and highlighted tolerability constraints in low-output, hypotension-prone patients [17].

The role of ARNI in heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction has been more nuanced. PARAMOUNT showed greater NT-proBNP reduction and left atrial reverse remodelling with LCZ696 than valsartan in HFpEF, encouraging phase III testing [18]. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite of total heart-failure hospitalisations and cardiovascular death, but suggested greater benefit in patients with lower ejection fraction and in women [19]. PARALLAX confirmed natriuretic peptide reduction but did not improve six-minute walk distance compared with individualized standard therapy [20]. Pooled analyses across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF indicate that treatment effect is greatest below the normal ejection-fraction range and attenuates as ejection fraction rises [21]. PARAGLIDE-HF, enrolling patients with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction after worsening heart failure, supported NT-proBNP reduction and possible clinical benefit in recently decompensated patients, especially toward the lower end of the “preserved” range [22]. By contrast, PARADISE-MI did not significantly reduce cardiovascular death or incident heart failure after acute myocardial infarction, so routine post-infarction substitution for ACE inhibition is not established [23].

Pharmacologically, sacubitril/valsartan has predictable exposure after oral dosing, and valsartan doses in the combination are more bioavailable than conventional valsartan formulations [24]. Earlier hypertension studies confirmed potent blood-pressure lowering, which explains both benefit and the common limiting adverse effect: symptomatic hypotension [25]. Implementation remains incomplete. Modelling suggested large preventable mortality if eligible HFrEF patients received ARNI [26], yet registry data documented underuse and underdosing of foundational HFrEF therapies [27]. Contemporary US and European guidelines therefore recommend ARNI as a foundational therapy for symptomatic chronic HFrEF, either as first-line renin–angiotensin system therapy or as replacement for ACE inhibitor/ARB, with a 36-hour washout after ACE inhibitors to reduce angioedema risk [28,29]. The 2022 US guideline also gives weaker recommendations for selected patients with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction, particularly when ejection fraction is at the lower end of those categories [30].

Overall, sacubitril/valsartan is a cornerstone of HFrEF management, with robust mortality and morbidity benefit, evidence supporting early initiation after stabilisation, and mechanistic links to reverse remodelling. Its value in HFpEF is more selective, concentrated in patients whose phenotype resembles HFrEF biologically or by ejection fraction. The central clinical task is no longer whether ARNI works in HFrEF, but how rapidly, safely and equitably it can be implemented.
